\chapter{Falsos Amigos --- the Words That Obey and Lie}
\label{ch:falsos-amigos}
\hlchaptermodality{66}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can spot a false friend by checking a decoded word against the sentence.}

Recognise exito, actualmente and libreria as words that obey the rules and mean something else.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[falsos amigos]{falsos amigos}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-falsos-amigos}



\begin{quote}
Every rule in this book has come with the same warning: a \textbf{lead}, not a guarantee.

Today is the chapter where the lead is wrong, on purpose.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the words that answer and lie}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{A false friend is not a word that breaks your rules. It is a word that obeys them and still means something else.}
\end{quote}

A word that resists every rule just looks foreign, and you look it up. A false friend hands you an answer with a straight face.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{your rule says} & \textbf{it actually means} \\
\midrule
\emph{éxito} & exit & \textbf{success} \\
\emph{actualmente} & actually & \textbf{currently} \\
\emph{librería} & library & \textbf{bookshop} \\
\emph{embarazada} & embarrassed & \textbf{pregnant} \\
\emph{ropa} & rope & \textbf{clothes} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Most are not coincidences.} They are roots the two languages shared and then walked away from:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{exitus} was \textbf{a going out}. English kept the door — \emph{exit}. Spanish kept the outcome: the way a thing \emph{came out}, then a good one. \textbf{Success.}
  \item Latin \emph{actuālis} was about \textbf{action}. Through Old French it came to mean \emph{now existing}; Spanish kept that time sense, and English kept going, to \emph{real}. Both moved — in different directions.
  \item A \emph{librería} is where \emph{libros} are: a \textbf{bookshop}. The building that lends them is a \emph{biblioteca}.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{One of the five is a genuine accident.} \emph{Ropa} is Germanic, from a word for \emph{plunder}; \emph{rope} is a different Germanic word. They did not drift apart — they collided. Both kinds exist.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{The rule is not \textquotedblleft{}distrust the rules.\textquotedblright{}} Your endings are still right about two thousand \emph{-ción} words. What this adds is a second question, asked \textbf{after} the ending answers:

\begin{quote}
Does the meaning fit what is being said?
\end{quote}

\emph{Estoy embarazada}, from someone apologising, is not \emph{I am embarrassed} — the sentence would be strange. The ending offered a candidate; the \textbf{context} rejected it. Five false friends is not a list to memorise. It is a \textbf{habit}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{éxito, actualmente, librería} — and what each really means
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What makes a false friend dangerous rather than merely hard? (It \textbf{obeys} your rules.) And what is the second question, after the ending answers? (\textbf{Does the meaning fit the sentence?})
\end{tcolorbox}
